## Neyman–Pearson: the likelihood ratio is all you need

Take $H_0$ = [$B$]{.B} (good batch) and $H_1$ = [$A$]{.A} (bad batch).

- **Type I error** $\alpha$: rejecting a good batch. **Type II error** $\beta$: accepting a bad one.

::: {.thm}
[Neyman–Pearson lemma (1933).]{.thm-title} Among all tests with type I error $\le\alpha$, the one with the smallest $\beta$ rejects $H_0$ when
$$
\frac{P(D\mid H_1)}{P(D\mid H_0)} > k \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{evidence for } H_1 > 10\log_{10}k \,\mathrm{dB}.
$$
:::

- Thresholding Jaynes' evidence is therefore the **optimal** frequentist test.
  - The two schools disagree on how to *choose* $k$: Jaynes uses prior odds and losses (Ch 13–14), Neyman–Pearson uses a fixed $\alpha$.

::: {.notes}
35:00–38:00. No proof; the idea is in the appendix (it is a short exchange argument). Main message: the frequentist "most powerful test" is the same evidence threshold.
:::

## Stein's lemma: KL is the error exponent

![](fig/v5_stein.svg){fig-align="center" width="1100"}

::: {.thm .small}
[Chernoff–Stein lemma.]{.thm-title} With $\alpha$ fixed, the best possible $\beta_n$ satisfies $\;\frac1n\log\beta_n \to -D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{H_0}\,\|\,P_{H_1})$.
:::

::: {.notes}
38:00–42:00. Left: β falls exponentially (a straight line in dB). Right: the per-widget rate approaches KL slowly, because there is a subexponential correction factor. Note which KL appears, D(P0‖P1): *expected evidence against H1 when H0 is true*, i.e. how fast an H0-world produces data that rule out H1. Stretch: Cover & Thomas §11.8.
:::

## Wald's SPRT is Jaynes' robot

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Sequential probability ratio test** (Wald, 1945):

- add up the log likelihood ratio one observation at a time
- stop the first time it leaves $(a, b)$

This is exactly the robot in §4.2, with $a=-13\,\mathrm{dB}$ and $b=0\,\mathrm{dB}$.

**Wald–Wolfowitz (1948):** no test with the same $\alpha,\beta$ uses fewer observations on average.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.ask}
**Wald's approximation:** $\mathbb{E}[N] \approx \dfrac{\text{distance to the boundary}}{\text{drift}}$. Estimate it for both hypotheses.
:::
::: {.fragment}
- [$A$ true]{.A}: $\dfrac{10\,\mathrm{dB}}{0.357} \approx 28$ widgets
- [$B$ true]{.B}: $\dfrac{3\,\mathrm{dB}}{0.306} \approx 10$ widgets

[Ignores overshoot and paths that hit the wrong boundary.]{.small .muted}
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
42:00–45:00. Tie it back to the random-walk slide: we just computed the expected run length of Jaynes' robot from KL. The robot rarely needs many widgets when the batch is good, because it starts at −10 dB.
:::

## The law of large numbers, applied to log-likelihood

Data $x_1,\dots,x_n$ come independently from $p_{\theta^\ast}$. For any $\theta$:
$$
\frac1n\log\frac{L(\theta)}{L(\theta^\ast)} = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \log\frac{p_\theta(x_i)}{p_{\theta^\ast}(x_i)}
\;\xrightarrow{\ \text{LLN}\ }\; \mathbb{E}_{\theta^\ast}\!\left[\log\frac{p_\theta}{p_{\theta^\ast}}\right] = -D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta^\ast\,\|\,\theta).
$$

::: {.fragment}
- The right-hand side is $<0$ for $\theta\ne\theta^\ast$ (Gibbs), so $L(\theta)/L(\theta^\ast)\approx e^{-nD_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta^\ast\,\|\,\theta)}\to 0$.
- So the likelihood (and therefore the posterior) piles up at $\theta^\ast$. This answers the question from the Bayes animation.
:::

::: {.notes}
45:00–47:00. One line of algebra, then the picture on the next slide.
:::

## KL and entropy

Let $u$ be uniform on $m$ outcomes. Then
$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\,\|\,u) = \sum_x p(x)\log\big(m\,p(x)\big) = \log m - H(p),\qquad H(p) = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x).
$$

- Maximising entropy is the same as **minimising the KL divergence from uniform**: choose the distribution that is hardest to tell apart from "know nothing".
- Ch 11 does this with constraints (MaxEnt), and Jaynes' general version replaces $u$ by a measure $m(x)$, giving $-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\,\|\,m)$.

## Teaser: information geometry

::: {}
Close together, KL behaves like a squared distance: $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta\,\|\,\theta+\delta)\approx\tfrac12 I(\theta)\,\delta^2$.
The Bernoulli family becomes a **quarter circle of length $\pi$**.

## A2: Fisher information from a Taylor expansion {.smaller}

Bernoulli: $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta\,\|\,\theta+\delta) = \theta\log\frac{\theta}{\theta+\delta} + (1-\theta)\log\frac{1-\theta}{1-\theta-\delta}$.

Expand $\log(1+u) = u - \tfrac{u^2}{2} + O(u^3)$:
$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta\,\|\,\theta+\delta) = \frac{\delta^2}{2\,\theta(1-\theta)} + O(\delta^3) = \tfrac12 I(\theta)\,\delta^2 + O(\delta^3),
\qquad I(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(\partial_\theta\log p_\theta\right)^2\right] = \frac{1}{\theta(1-\theta)}.
$$
(Checked in Wolfram Language.)

- **Bernstein–von Mises.** Posterior $\approx \mathcal N\!\left(\hat\theta,\ \frac{1}{n\,I(\theta^\ast)}\right)$ for large $n$.
- **Geometry.** $ds^2 = I(\theta)\,d\theta^2$. With $\theta = \sin^2\phi$ we get $ds = 2\,d\phi$, so $[0,1]$ has length $\int_0^1\frac{d\theta}{\sqrt{\theta(1-\theta)}} = \pi$. The Jeffreys prior $\propto\sqrt{I(\theta)}$ is Beta($\tfrac12,\tfrac12$).
- **Three outcomes:** $p\mapsto 2\sqrt{p}$ sends the simplex to an octant of a sphere of radius 2. **Gaussian** $(\mu,\sigma)$: the Poincaré half-plane.

## A3: Neyman–Pearson in one line {.smaller}

Let $\phi^\ast$ be the likelihood-ratio test ($\phi^\ast = 1$ when $p_1 > k p_0$), and let $\phi$ be any other test with $\mathbb{E}_0\phi\le\mathbb{E}_0\phi^\ast=\alpha$. Then
$$
\sum_D (\phi^\ast - \phi)(p_1 - k\,p_0) \;\ge\; 0
$$
because the two factors always have the same sign. Rearranging gives $\mathbb{E}_1\phi^\ast - \mathbb{E}_1\phi \ge k(\mathbb{E}_0\phi^\ast - \mathbb{E}_0\phi) \ge 0$, so $\phi^\ast$ has at least as much power.
